shows.desc: This episode of *Africa Now*, hosted by Mwiza Munthali, centers on a rare 2005 interview with Alice Coltrane — conducted at her Los Angeles home by KPFK's Maggie LaPique and Pacifica Radio Archives producer Mark Torres — that exists nowhere else but the Pacifica archive. In it, Alice describes first encountering John at a Detroit concert where he was leaning on a table "holding his forehead, pensive," recalls the two of them staying up after their children went to sleep to read through scores by Stravinsky and Schoenberg, and recounts how John wrote letters to Congressman Conyers and Dick Gregory during the civil rights era urging financial empowerment for Black people — letters that, she says, got no useful answer. The episode aired as part of WPFW's daylong centennial tribute, *A Love Supreme: John Coltrane at 100*, with program director Katea Stitt joining Munthali to discuss the archive documentary and co-host James Pope providing the framing essay connecting Coltrane's music to the broader tradition of African diasporic expression.

Ellen Carter hosts this two-hour block of WPFW's all-day John Coltrane centennial tribute, built around the theme of Coltrane's spiritual and romantic sides. The hour's most distinctive moment is a 2024 interview Carter conducted with saxophonist Lakecia Benjamin, who describes knowing Alice Coltrane's music before John Coltrane's and wanting to "equal the playing field" between them on her album *Pursuance: The Coltranes* — recorded after a car accident whose wreckage, Carter says, made survival seem unimaginable. The program moves through selections spanning Coltrane's career, from his first recorded solo with Dizzy Gillespie's band on March 1, 1951, to the *A Love Supreme* quartet sides with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones, to a 1956 session with Kenny Drew and Philly Joe Jones, closing with a local Washington ensemble's rendition of Coltrane's "Equinox."

shows.desc: Kofi Kissi Dompere's *African Rhythms and Extensions* moves through a late-night set that travels from Ghana to Nigeria, the Republic of the Congo, Angola, Senegal, and South Africa, playing highlife, Makossa, Soukous, and related styles — with the host naming specific artists including Franco on guitar and bassist Johnny Deyan, whose track he dedicates to Abdullah Ibrahim. Dompere briefly steps outside the music to note that the Kente and Adinkra symbols carry epistemic structures behind each motif, and that "rhythm is a power of the nature." The program closes with a spoken-word piece tracing the passage of enslaved Africans across the sea and their descendants' lives in America — from working "from morn till night" without human rights to children "born with no last names" — framed around the phrase "American fruit with African roots."

*Back to Paradise* with Byron "B-Note" Brown moves through two hours of house music, with Brown pausing mid-show to reel off the full playlist: tracks by Inner City, Louie Vega, CeCe Peniston, Estelle, and a Junior Vasquez remix of Lisa Lisa sit alongside newer vocals from Tasha LaRay and Merlin Bobb. Brown closes with a tribute to the house vocalists who shaped the culture — Ultra Naté, Inaya Day, Tracy Hamlin, Monique Bingham among them — and a shout-out to DJ Spin's benefit show, where Kenny Dope, Terry Hunter, and Baltimore's Teddy Douglas all appeared.

shows.desc: **Climate Friday** host Reverend Yearwood, president of the Hip-Hop Caucus, explains how petrochemical plants sited along an 85-mile stretch between Baton Rouge and New Orleans — a corridor known as Cancer Alley — are producing cancer rates at the highest levels in the country, predominantly killing Black residents, and how activists used Louisiana burial-ground laws to block companies from building on former plantation sites. Yearwood also discusses the Netflix documentary *Plastic Detox*, which followed families who removed plastics from their homes and, in several cases, reversed infertility, and he draws a direct line between Cancer Alley, data centers being placed in low-income Black neighborhoods from Memphis to Baltimore, and what he calls a business plan that amounts to a death sentence for those communities.

shows.desc: Host Daman Harris opens this episode of *You Must Learn* with a "This Week in Black History" segment noting that in 1957 Louis Armstrong publicly condemned the federal government's failure to protect the Little Rock Nine and refused a State Department tour abroad in protest — then draws a line from that moment to the 1963 bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church that killed four Black girls. The episode then introduces Amy Watkins, a new co-host and children's author who wrote a character with albinism after a student in her classroom had the condition, and features Tara Liebert of Free Minds Book Club — founded at the dying request of Glenn McGinnis, executed in 2000 at age 17 after writing from death row to ask for a book club for incarcerated youth — who describes the organization's Read for Youth Justice reading list, including its section on children with incarcerated parents. The hour closes with Richard Rogers, a principal leadership coach three weeks into his role at Prince George's County Public Schools, reflecting on 33 years in education and describing being repeatedly assigned to high-need schools as a Black man on the assumption he could "wave a magic wand" — while being denied the option of leading more affluent ones.

shows.desc: Host Sam PK Collins of *All Eyes on DC* spent the hour with attorney Thomas T. Ruffin analyzing the federal bribery trial of Ward 8 DC Councilmember Trayvon White. Ruffin walked through two specific Supreme Court cases shaping the defense — the McDonnell case, which he said established that a public official can receive money in exchange for services they would ordinarily perform without that constituting bribery, and *Matthews v. United States* (485 U.S. 58, 1988), which allows a defendant to argue simultaneously that he did not take a bribe and that he was entrapped into taking one. The conversation also covered the jury's composition — nine white jurors out of fourteen — FBI audio and video recorded in Kamara's car, and callers' concerns about whether the prosecution reflects a broader federal effort to undermine Black political power in DC.

Hosted by Weza Muntali, this episode of *Africa Now* features a July panel discussion held at Sankofa Video Books and Cafe marking the 50th anniversary of the Soweto Uprising. Twigs Apple, who was expelled from the University of Fort Hare after 1976 for his membership in the South African Students Organization, describes how the uprising spread from Soweto to Port Elizabeth on August 18th of that year — the same day Steve Biko and Peter Jones were stopped at a roadblock, leading to Biko's death by September 12th. Dr. Sylvia Hill, a co-founder of the Southern Africa Support Project and a leader of the Free South Africa Movement, traces the organizing that led to the 6th Pan-African Congress in Dar es Salaam in 1974, including a conversation she had with President Nyerere in which he told her, "You can make any kind of decision you want to because you're political — you don't have to feed people." Dr. Greg Carr of Howard University moderates, drawing connections between the 1976 generation's fight against Afrikaans-language instruction and present-day South Africa's unresolved questions of land ownership, unemployment, and political education.

shows.desc: This episode of *African Rhythms and Extensions*, hosted by Kofi Kissi Dompere, is dedicated to John Coltrane's 100th birthday anniversary, framing his expansion of jazz harmony and his role as a spiritual voice during the Black liberation struggles of the 1960s as rooted in the power of African polyrhythm. The program moves geographically through music from Eritrea, Kenya, Guinea, the Republic of the Congo, Senegal, Togo, Sierra Leone, and Cameroon, with tracks including work by Mongo Santamaria and Armando Peraza alongside Congolese rumba and Cuban rhythmic traditions. Dompere closes with a reminder — "if you are drinking, don't drive; if you are driving, don't drink" — and a call for cooperation over confrontation before handing off to the next program.

Derrick "D-Train" Coleman hosts this two-hour house music set on *Back to Paradise*, opening with a brief reflection on the 25th anniversary of September 11th before moving into the music. Hour one runs through tracks including Margaret Grace's "Circle of Life," a Timmy Register rework of "You Brought the Sunshine," and Dinga Daba's remix of "I Feel for You," while hour two brings in a Timmy Register and Adam Rios remix of The Police's "Wrapped Around Your Finger" alongside sets from Julian Gomes, Ultra Nate, and a closing stretch with Stacey Kidd's "The Situation."

shows.desc: Mississippi artist Dear Silas talked with co-host Brittany Bell-Serrat about his two simultaneously released projects, *Sophisticated Ratchet Red* (hip-hop) and *Sophisticated Ratchet Blue* (jazz), explaining that the name "Sophisticated Ratchet" is about disrupting expectations and showing up authentically — and pushed back on negative narratives about Mississippi, arguing that "racism ain't regional" and that Mississippi is one of the Blackest states in the country. Later, Jharrel Clay of Hip Hop Caucus spoke with Dominique Morgan — a Black trans woman, former content creator for Apple, and former head of Black and Pink National, where she grew the budget from $225,000 to $3.2 million — about Black trans identity, incarceration, voting as one tool among many for community change, and why she believes telling people what to do at the ballot box backfires compared to helping people make informed decisions on their own terms.

shows.desc: Dr. Jeffrey Johnson, coordinator of Black Men's Health at the African American Health Program, told host Dr. Daryl Howard that the average Black man lives 70.8 years compared to 75.8 years for white men, and described how "sustained high-intensity trauma" — a term coined by physician Dr. Tali Elliott — and a "weathering effect" can make a 65-year-old Black man biologically closer to 68. Johnson also discussed the Tuskegee Experiment's lasting grip on medical mistrust, his program's strategy of bringing health screenings to barbershops, salons, and basketball courts, and a free Community Ambassador Training coming up Saturday from 9 a.m. to noon. In the second segment, Kim Bishop and Troy Bishop described Good Hope Union UMC in Colesville, Montgomery County, a church founded in 1870 by three freed Black farmers — John Powell, Tom Stewart, and Sam Jones — who purchased land from Sarah Watts; its congregation includes the first ordained African American female pastor in the Baltimore-Washington Conference of the United Methodist Church and a Negro Leagues pitcher who caught with the Newark Eagles, Birmingham Black Barons, and Atlanta Black Crackers, and the Bishops described plans to restore the 1913 sanctuary, ring its bell again, and host a free community health bazaar on September 19th.

Jackie Carter, founder of Children's Legacy Theater, describes workshopping the Secure D.C. bill line-by-line with 30 Ward 8 youth who then wrote three-minute testimonies to deliver to the D.C. Council — and explains how pairing that civic work with historical productions like *The Meeting* (which imagines a conversation between Dr. King and Malcolm X) and *Fannie Lou Hamer: Until I'm Free* motivates students who previously struggled with school attendance. Host Sam P.K. Collins also interviews Carter and program manager Brittany Sestare about their summer program in which student playwrights wrote, cast, and directed their peers in original works, and about Carter's pitch at a Janice Lewis George listening forum that Ward 8 needs dedicated space on the St. Elizabeths campus for arts nonprofits — noting that in 2016 the arts brought $10.6 billion into D.C. The episode opens with Collins's on-the-ground interview with mayoral candidate Lewis George about her plans to use mayoral control of schools to address chronic absenteeism, literacy gaps, and special-education delivery.

Africa Now host Mueezza Muntali presents an archival recording of a post-screening discussion held at Sankofa Video, Books, and Café in Washington, D.C., where Howard University Africana Studies professor Dr. Greg Carr argued that the Wayne Frederick Undergraduate Library across from Howard "doesn't have a single book in it," called the university structure itself "death," and described students at Philadelphia Freedom Schools being given Cedric Robinson and other demanding texts regardless of reading level — "we're going to bleed on these pages." The conversation, moderated by Africa Now executive producer James Pope, grew out of a screening of the documentary *How to Build a Library*, which follows two Kenyan women who took over management of Nairobi's Macmillan Memorial Library — a whites-only space from its 1931 founding until independence — and attempted to decolonize it. Audience members at Sankofa, including a Howard professor who learned to read at Chicago's Institute of Positive Education and a woman who taught all three of her children to read before kindergarten, joined the exchange over what it means to build a library as an institution of memory recovery rather than simply recover one.

shows.desc: Climate Friday host Cross the Producer interviews Dr. Sokobe Wilson — founder of CEJA Inc. and professor at the University of Maryland School of Public Health — who details how data centers like Elon Musk's Colossus 1 facility in Boxtown, a Freedmen's community in Memphis, are burning natural gas turbines in a neighborhood that already has a cancer rate four times the national average, while hyperscale facilities elsewhere consume roughly five million gallons of water a day and generate low-frequency noise that, unlike high-frequency sound, bounces over physical barriers and can travel far enough to disrupt sleep for miles around. The conversation also covers the disproportionate impact of power outages and energy shutoffs on Black communities — drawing a line from redlining to the two-week outage in Gary, Indiana — and previews Dr. Wilson's 12th annual Environmental Justice and Health Disparities Symposium, themed "EJ 2076: Make America Just Again," running September 14–19 with keynotes from Justin Pearson and Peggy Shepard and in-person sessions at Bowie State University.

Vaughn Bennett, a DC firefighter turned 25-year chess instructor who has taught more than 7,000 children, explains on this episode of *#YouMustLearn* how the DC Chess League excluded Black DC residents from tournaments, scholarships, and leadership for nearly 80 years — a history the US Chess Federation itself documented in a 2022 report. The episode also features Baba Oso, a founding member of Kankuran West African Dance and Music Company, previewing the group's 43rd-anniversary performance at Crampton Auditorium at Howard University and tracing the banning of the drum under slavery to its role as a communication and healing tool. A third guest, Natani Victoria Lim of Embracing Equity, describes the Albuquerque-based nonprofit's virtual workshops on building cultures of belonging in schools and its debate over whether to remove equity-related language from its website under current political pressure — a debate the team resolved by keeping the name and the mission intact.

Marcellus Queen, founder and executive director of Representation for the Bottom and a former youth development worker at D.C.'s Youth Services Center, tells host Sam PK Collins how the facility houses children with serious mental health conditions alongside general-population youth, with no padded rooms, undertrained staff, and a ratio that can leave one worker responsible for 15 kids — and describes throwing his keys to a detained youth during an 8-on-1 fight to get him into a safe room, the act that ultimately cost him his job. Queen also reflects on the recent death of his longtime collaborator Shama King, whom he found dead the day after the two of them gave out 300 pairs of Jordans to youth at a back-to-school event. The episode opens with local news items including D.C. mayoral nominee Janice Lewis George's eight-ward listening tour and a D.C. Council hearing scheduled for September 24th on the Vaccine Administration Protection Amendment Act, which would shield local healthcare providers from liability for vaccine-related injuries.

This Labor Day episode of *Africa Now*, hosted by Mueza Muntali, draws from the program's archive to air a panel discussion on the first point of the Southern Workers Power Program: the right to organize, collectively bargain, and strike. Destiny Blackwell, an Amazon worker organizing with CAUSE (Carolina Amazonians United for Solidarity and Empowerment) in Garner, North Carolina, describes coworkers sleeping in their cars and missing rent while working for what she calls the richest company in the world, and argues that Amazon's tax cuts for employing HBCU students and disabled workers amount to subsidies that should instead go directly to workers' wages. Chris Hollis of Black Workers for Justice and UE 150 recounts how Virginia Beach municipal workers staged an illegal wildcat stoppage at Waste Management on a Wednesday — the day upper-class residents needed trash pickup — and won new equipment, a 10% raise, and eventually a $15 minimum wage after attending every city council meeting. Historian Robin D.G. Kelley traces how Jim Crow segregation and right-to-work laws were ruling-class responses to interracial labor organizing, using the example of the largely African American female Local 22 of the Food, Tobacco, and Agriculture and Allied Workers Union at RJ Reynolds in Winston-Salem, which fought sexual harassment and launched voter registration drives before the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 stripped unions of much of that power.

shows.desc: Heather McTeer Toney — former mayor of Greenville, Mississippi, former EPA Region 4 Administrator, and Executive Director of Beyond Petrochemicals — tells host Brittany Bell-Serrat that petrochemical pollution is "if not already, the number one driver of increased emissions," and describes how Beyond Petrochemicals works in Louisiana, Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and West Virginia by following communities that identify themselves as overburdened rather than "parachuting in." Toney, who was serving as mayor during Hurricane Katrina and watched displaced residents arrive in Greenville, connects that experience to her argument that race and economic inequality cannot be separated from climate response. The conversation also covers the role of Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, the HBCU Climate Change Consortium, and Black churches as entry points for broadening climate organizing, and touches on the deaths of Nolan Wells and Tayshia Fortune and what Toney, as the mother of two Black sons, calls the need to break "the repetition of the behavior."

On the August 27th episode of *#YouMustLearn*, host Dr. Daryl Howard opens with a detailed account of the Haitian Revolution — including Toussaint L'Ouverture's capture after being lured to a meeting under a false promise of safety, and how a lieutenant "a little over 20" finished the fight and declared independence in 1804 — before bringing on Baba Ayise and Dr. Azoma Miller, a professor of African American Studies at Ohio University, to discuss a Black August webinar they are co-hosting through the Asen of Kemet, an African-centered fraternity founded at Morehouse as an alternative to the Divine Nine. The two guests argue that figures like George Jackson, Assata Shakur, and Fred Hampton are largely absent from mainstream education, and that efforts to remove exhibits about George Washington enslaving Africans at his Philadelphia house show that erasure is active, not just passive. In the second segment, Mazi Mutafa, executive director of the nearly 25-year-old hip-hop nonprofit Words, Beats & Life, describes their upcoming Game Day — an intergenerational free event built around chess, checkers, dominoes, Uno, spades, mahjong, and video games — and explains that this summer was the first since 2020 when young people in their programs again told staff they had made friends with kids from other neighborhoods they had never met.

Dr. LaJoy Johnson-Law, Ward 8's representative on the D.C. State Board of Education, tells host Brother Sam P.K. Collins how she first got into advocacy after her daughter A'Bria — born at 23 weeks and one pound six ounces — stopped receiving her special education services, leading Johnson-Law to file a complaint with OSSE and eventually testify before the D.C. Council. She also explains why she pushed the State Board to pass a resolution on real ID access for students, arguing that with National Guard, FBI, and other federal law enforcement now visibly present near Ward 8 schools, high schoolers who look older than their age need documentation beyond a school ID. The episode also covers the fourth consecutive year of CAPE standardized test score gains, including double-digit math increases at Savoy Elementary and Gar-Field Elementary, and Johnson-Law breaks down why she believes chronic absenteeism data misleads by lumping excused and unexcused absences together without asking why students are missing school.

Hosted by Weza Muntali, this *Africa Now* episode airs an archival conversation with Professor Gaye McDougall — who served six years as the first UN Special Rapporteur on Minority Issues, sat on the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, and helped shape the 2001 Durban Conference — in which she explains how George Floyd's murder provided the final push to get the UN Permanent Forum on People of African Descent "across the goal line" after Western countries had been dragging their feet on its adoption. McDougall describes walking into the Forum's December 2022 Geneva launch and finding the same room she had first entered decades earlier — when she was the only person from the African diaspora present — now filled with 600 to 700 people of African descent from around the world. She also breaks down the Forum's ten-member composition, its uncertain relationship to the General Assembly versus the Human Rights Council, and why she calls its founding resolution "a blank piece of paper" — one that leaves its members to define their own power on reparations and beyond.

shows.desc: Host Rev Yearwood convened a conversation about Washington, D.C.'s "teen takeover" media narrative with Yasmin Salina, co-founder of the Hustlers Guild, and Nicole Newman, executive director of Critical Exposure — who cited a city racial equity assessment finding that young people who have a first contact with police are 121 times more likely to have a repeated negative interaction. Salina, a sixth-generation Washingtonian building school-to-career pipelines through sports and entertainment, argued that it costs over $35,000 a year to keep someone in prison while organizations serving hundreds of youth are often given the same amount in grants. Newman, whose organization has worked with D.C. youth on campaigns ranging from school facilities funding to mental health resources, described how young people themselves are pushing back on the curfew and calling for free transportation, family-sized housing, and year-round workforce development programs similar to the Summer Youth Employment Program.

The #YouMustLearn program on WPFW features an interview with genealogist and author Andre Kearns, a Washington D.C. native who traces his family back to Emmanuel and Joan Cumbo — captives from the Kingdom of Ndongo in present-day Angola who arrived at Port Comfort around 1628 — and to his third great-grandfather William B. Harvell, who was sold as a child named Buck in an 1832 bill of sale and went on after emancipation to become a landowner, found a church, and establish a school that launched five generations of HBCU attendance in Kearns's family, with a sixth generation now at Howard. The episode also covers the DiverseCITY Fund's fall grant cycle, open to Black and brown-led organizations with budgets under $50,999 that do organizing, advocacy, or healing justice work in D.C., with board member Nkechi Feaster — who first encountered the fund while living in a family shelter at D.C. General — explaining how the fund's community grantmaking model deliberately removes barriers that typically block impacted residents from both funding decisions and funding itself. A third segment previews WPFW's 5th annual 5K walk/run on September 12th at Bladensburg Waterfront Park, where holistic health practitioner and Black Love Day founder Mama Ayo Handy Kendi describes new additions including walking meditation and strength training.

Matt Miller, program coordinator for District Dads at Martha's Table, joins host Brother Sam PK Collins to discuss an upcoming men's fashion showcase at the organization's Outfitters clothing boutique on Martin Luther King Avenue — where alumni dads will model four scenes of four different styles, and where all clothing is available to community members at no cost. Miller explains that the event grew out of his observation that men in the community are "walking around looking like bank robbers," and argues that dressing with purpose can shift community narratives; he also describes District Dads' 17-week fatherhood curriculum, which draws participants ages 16 to 77 and closes with five weeks focused on emotional wellness. The episode's second segment features Xavier Brown and Jamila White of the Black Environmental Fellowship, a six-week summer program for youth from east of the Anacostia River that included a freedom tour to Harriet Tubman's birthplace on the Eastern Shore, a visit to Black-owned land formerly used to enslave ancestors, camping in Southern Maryland, and a closing ceremony where fellows presented on the Kwanzaa principles — wearing sashes handmade in Accra — to their community.

This episode of *Africa Now*, hosted by Weza Muntali, features a conversation with writer Arun Kundnani about the political life of Jamil Al-Amin, formerly known as H. Rap Brown — including the detail that, when FBI files obtained through Freedom of Information requests listed Al-Amin's possessions at the time of his arrests, the books he was carrying were works by Nkrumah, Fanon, and Robert Williams. Kundnani traces how Al-Amin, elected SNCC chair at 23 and named in J. Edgar Hoover's 1967 COINTELPRO memo alongside three others, argued at the National Conference for New Politics that Black people constituted "an internal colony" and that America was enacting genocide through Vietnam draft casualties, child poverty, mass incarceration, and disproportionate targeting in reproductive health. The conversation also covers Al-Amin's conversion to Islam in the New York State prison system in 1971, his argument that Islam made activists "COINTELPRO-proof," and his organizing alongside Puerto Rican and Chicano movements — all framed around Kundnani's ongoing biography project, the first of its kind on Al-Amin.

shows.desc: **Climate Friday** host Rev. Yearwood interviews Dr. Lemire Toran, a Howard University professor in its new Department of Earth, Environment, and Equity, about his recently published book *Unlearned Power: Strengthening Communities in the Age of Environmental Crisis*. Toran describes how the book moves from the Onondaga Nation through communities across the country to argue that "unlearned power" means both rethinking literal energy systems and dismantling the political and socioeconomic arrangements that have placed Black, brown, and Indigenous communities in what Yearwood calls "the path of least resistance" — and he recounts the episode in which a major petrochemical company called the FBI on him simply for writing a report on human health impacts. Yearwood also discusses his own role producing climate documentaries including *Plastic Detox*, currently on Netflix, and his appearance at the NABJ conference in Atlanta, where he argued that the progressive climate movement is in a "crisis of imagination" and must do better at storytelling and narrative.

shows.desc: This episode of *Cuba Libre* on WPFW is a daylong fundraising broadcast marking the centennial birthday of Fidel Castro, anchored by a curated mix from DJ Abby she calls "ajiaco" — named for a Cuban stew she describes as a metaphor for the Cuban people, contrasting Cuba's blending of "multiple elements and textures" with America's melting pot model of homogenization. The mix features two all-women salsa orchestras, Son Damas and Orquesta Anacoana, alongside artists including Los Van Van, Daimé Arocena, Ibeji, and Bobby Céspedes, whose closing song *Si Agua No Llueve, Maíz No Crece* ("If it doesn't rain, corn doesn't grow") DJ Abby frames as both a commentary on current conditions and a call to lift the U.S. blockade on Cuba. The host, identified as Katea Stitt, notes that later in the day she will be in conversation with Alice Walker and Andy Shallal about Cuba and Castro, whom Walker met many times.

shows.desc: This special edition of *Life Music*, hosted by Saiz Kamaluddin, aired as part of a full 24-hour WPFW tribute to Cuba timed to the centennial birthday of Fidel Castro, running from midnight to 2 a.m. The playlist drew on Celia Cruz, Tito Puente, Orquesta Revé, Harry Belafonte, the Fania All-Stars, Pancho Sanchez, Johnny Pacheco, Pérez Prado's "Patricia," and Kenny Dorham's "Aphrodisiac" from his album *Afro-Cuban*. Between sets, Kamaluddin noted that later in the day listeners would hear stories and information about current conditions in Cuba and ways to help.

Jawana Hardy, a U.S. Air Force veteran and founder of Guns Down Friday, describes watching National Guard and FBI agents pull a teenager off a Lime bike to harass him, and recounts how youth she had organized through a Know Your Rights training — led by Black Swan Academy — successfully turned away FBI agents the very next day, only to have those agents taunt the kids with the names of incarcerated friends. Host Brother Sam PK Collins also speaks with poet Janari Mitchell, who describes being handcuffed by four Park Police officers at Anacostia Metro Station on June 29th — the first day of a summer youth employment program — had her shoelaces and shorts drawstring removed, and was held at the Park Police station at Haines Point for hours before charges were dropped, which she identifies as a pattern of data collection and surveillance targeting Black youth. Both guests speak specifically about communities east of the Anacostia River during the one-year mark of what Collins calls the federal occupation of Washington, DC.

This episode of *Africa Now*, hosted by Mueezam Muntali, features a recorded panel discussion from Busboys and Poets in which journalist and author Linda Penzey-Gunther and Maurice Carney, executive director of Friends of the Congo, trace the uranium supply chain from the Shinkolobwe mine in the Belgian Congo — where ore graded at roughly 65% purity compared to 0.5% in Canada or Czechoslovakia — through the Manhattan Project and into present-day conflict over the DRC's minerals. Penzey-Gunther reads from her book *No to Nuclear* on the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, a covert Israeli operation called Operation Plumbat that smuggled Congolese uranium to the Dimona nuclear center, and the Navajo miners who were told uranium extraction was their "patriotic duty" while working without protective gear and are now surrounded by at least 500 abandoned mines on their land. The episode also includes a pledge-drive segment in which the show dedicates its fundraising goal to WPFW's first program director, Denise Oliver-Vélez, described as a Young Lord and Black Panther.

shows.desc: This episode of Climate Friday, hosted by producer DeJuan Cross, features Sharon Lavine and her daughter Shamaya Lavine-Davey of Rise St. James, the grassroots organization fighting petrochemical expansion in St. James Parish, Louisiana — where Sharon describes founding the group after Louisiana's governor approved a Formosa Plastics facility two miles from her home in 2018. Sharon recounts how Rise St. James uncovered ancestral burial grounds on the proposed plant site, brought evidence including a book of ancestors' names compiled by an archaeologist to the parish council 17 months before Formosa did, and watched the council side with industry anyway; Shamaya then explains that a judge revoked Formosa's air permits in 2022, the decision was overturned on appeal, and Rise St. James is now seeking a Supreme Court appeal while new EPA rules limiting ethylene oxide emissions have put the project's economic viability in doubt. The episode also includes Rev Yearwood's TED Talk arguing that the climate movement suffers from a "crisis of imagination" — that it communicates from "the rage of the privileged" rather than from the communities dying from petrochemical pollution along Cancer Alley's 85-mile stretch between Baton Rouge and New Orleans — and closes with a conversation about the temporary federal pause on LNG permitting and the fossil fuel industry's practice of withdrawing school funding, including a computer lab and dance uniforms at a local high school, after losing a fight to build.

Baba Eze's program #YouMustLearn features an interview with Cliff of Cartel Bussy, co-founder of Blue Montessori, a tuition-free Montessori school in its third year on Marion Barry Avenue in Anacostia, who explains how he incorporates go-go drumming and HBCU-style marching into his work with 3-to-6-year-olds and argues that Montessori's emphasis on self-direction maps directly onto the demands of college and the workplace. The second segment brings in film director Ime Atuk, whose film *Outdoor School* — screening August 15th at the George Washington University Student Center as part of the ADIFF DC festival — tells the true story of a 12-year-old boy in 1994 Portland, Oregon who is living under a tree with his mother and sister while protecting a pair of neon Deion Sanders patent leather Nike shoes; Atuk describes how audiences at screenings have been so affected by the film's treatment of domestic violence that he began distributing a resource guide, and recounts meeting a 12-year-old boy outside a theater in Ashland, Oregon whose family turned out to be in a situation mirroring the film's story.

David Black, a DC native who served 26 years in prison for a 1997 murder he says he did not commit, joined the inaugural episode of *All Eyes on DC* live — and was pulled over by three police cars mid-interview, receiving a ticket for being on his phone while his car was in park. Black discussed the pending motion to vacate his conviction, which cites witness intimidation, recanted statements, and prosecutorial suppression of evidence, and described his failed attempts to reach organizations including Roc Nation for help while incarcerated. The episode also featured Brother Johannes of Pan-African Community Action, who explained the group's new People's Transit Solidarity Program — launching August 8th at Anacostia Metro Station with free SmarTrip card distribution — as part of a broader strategy of community control over public infrastructure in Southeast DC. Host Sam P.K. Collins closed by invoking Mumia Abu-Jamal and Ida B. Wells, framing the show as a platform for Black journalism that refuses to be "watered down."

In an extended conversation with Dr. Janaína Oliveira — a film curator, film scholar, and activist visiting Washington from Brazil — *Africa Now* host Mwiza Munthali maps Brazil's political landscape ahead of October 4th general elections, with Oliveira tracing how four years of Bolsonaro's presidency damaged the country's public education and health systems, how his co-conspirators in the January 2023 coup attempt ended up in jail alongside ordinary participants, and why she considers Brazil's all-digital election system the best in the world. Oliveira also discusses Brazil's high rates of feminicide and the Lula government's shift toward state-led prevention campaigns, and notes that polls show Lula favored to defeat Jair Bolsonaro's son Flávio in the upcoming race, even as a bank corruption scheme implicating the Bolsonaro family continues to unfold.

shows.desc: Climate Friday host Rev Yearwood and co-host Brittany mark the 18th anniversary of the Respect My Vote campaign — launched in 2008 at the 930 Club near Howard University — with a recap of Brittany's interview with Hip Hop Caucus managing director and COO Liz Halstad, who discussed continuous voter engagement and what Brittany calls the deliberate "silencing of the data" around close elections in Mississippi. The hosts also walk through the history and meaning of Black August, tracing its roots to incarcerated organizers at San Quentin State Prison in 1979 and connecting it to events from the Haitian Revolution to Hurricane Katrina, while Rev Yearwood describes his personal practice of walking 5 miles a day — 2.5 miles to a coffee shop and back — as a way of managing grief after his mother's death on May Day, and the conversation extends to heat safety and the climate justice dimensions of extreme summer temperatures hitting even Southern California with unfamiliar humidity.

Host Daman Harris's show "You Must Learn" on WPFW features Curtis Valentine, founding president of the Male Educator Network and Policy Institute, discussing his book *Real Men Teach*, which traces Black male educators from John Chavis — a free Black man who taught white students in the early 1800s and whose student became a U.S. Senator from North Carolina — through Valentine's own great-grandfather, who co-founded a Rosenwald School, to figures such as Charles Ogletree, with testimony from former students including U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock and Governor Deval Patrick. The episode also features Baba Clifton of Mommy's TLC, an out-of-school-time program that has reached over 16,000 children in 25 years, announcing a pre-celebration at 2616 Georgia Avenue Northwest on August 1st, and Dr. Sekou Africa of Bowie State University, who describes building a pipeline for Black male educators from 8th grade through master's degree level and discusses how his own experience with burnout — including symptoms he mistook for a stroke and a heart attack — shaped his new initiative, the Black Male Educator Classroom.

On this episode of *Africa Now*, hosted by Mwiza Munthali, Dr. Ayize Sabater — founder of Mommy's TLC and the Black Montessori Education Fund — explains how his organization has given away nearly a quarter of a million dollars in mini grants to fund Black people entering Montessori education, reaching families and schools in the U.S., the Caribbean, and countries including The Gambia, Senegal, Nigeria, and Kenya. He traces his path from opening an independent African-centered school in Atlanta in September 1992, four months after graduating from Morehouse, to running a vegetarian restaurant chain called Delights of the Garden on Georgia Avenue across from Howard University, to arguing that Montessori's century-old model was deliberately sidelined in favor of a Prussian factory system designed for conformity over critical thinking. The episode also includes reporting from Ituri, DRC, where Congolese journalist Akili Mali Chomachoma and Stella Ramazani of the Basanja Coalition, with Maurice Carney of Friends of the Congo, describe an Ebola outbreak whose official death toll was approaching 1,000 but whose real count, they say, is likely three to five times higher — with a displacement camp of roughly 25,000 people near Bunia recording 57 suspected deaths before a single case was officially confirmed.

Hosted by Paulina Vassilian, this episode of *Capitalism, Race, and Democracy* centers on a July 21st walkout by Bay Area ILWU Local 10 longshoremen who shut down West Coast ports to honor the picket line at the C&H Sugar refinery in Crockett, California — where the Fanjul family's company bused in replacement workers and, according to a striker on tape, a scab driver plowed through the crowd and fled. A Filipino community organizer explains that the sugar aboard the ship *Tia Herald* comes from Negros Occidental in the Philippines, where armed forces under Marcos Jr. massacred 19 people in April, including a Filipino-American Bay Area activist named Lal Frijoles. The episode also features Greg Mitre, president of the ILWU Southern California Pensioners, arguing that automation has already eliminated 400 to 500 jobs at the Maersk terminal alone and warning that pairing AI with automation will leave no one left to consume or sustain the economy; and ATU Local 1208 president Charles Torrence Jr., whose 60-member Jackson, Mississippi transit local was in its third week striking against contractor MV Transportation over wages, seniority rights, and MV's proposal to eliminate two fixed routes and Saturday service.

Project Censored co-hosts Eleanor Goldfield and Mickey Huff lead two interviews on surveillance and artificial intelligence. First, Ed from Deflock explains how Flock Safety's automatic license plate readers function as a national database of vehicle images — searchable by color, make, bumper stickers, and dents — and documents how that data has been used for immigration enforcement, abortion monitoring, and by police officers stalking ex-girlfriends; he notes that California and Illinois laws barring ICE from accessing the data have been routinely broken, and that over 80 ALPR contracts have been canceled through community organizing, including in Austin and Denver. Then climate communicator Heidi Lim of AI Resist List walks through nine pillars of resistance to large-scale generative AI — including a tool called Nightshade that poisons training data, a map tracking over $1 billion in tech-company funding of newsrooms, and the Te Hiku Media project, in which a Māori-owned organization built a small language model trained on community-consented data to preserve the Māori language without relying on Silicon Valley infrastructure.

Abby Rozner, author of *Psychedelics and the Counterculture of Aging*, told host David Rabin that she interviewed 36 elders who were using psilocybin and other psychedelics to make peace with mortality, heal trauma, and build community — and that she found them easily by attending integration circles hosted by local psychedelic societies. She explained that ibogaine, a sacred medicine from the Bwiti people of Gabon, reached the Trump administration through a chain that ran from Rick Perry to Joe Rogan to Trump himself, and raised the question of who profits when indigenous intellectual property moves into pharmaceutical development. The second half of the hour shifted to Mosaic Theater's 2025-26 season, with Artistic Director Reginald Douglas describing three productions including *Somewhere Over the Border* — playwright Bryan Quijada's retelling of his Salvadoran mother's immigration story as *The Wizard of Oz*, with cumbia, mariachi, hip-hop, and rock — and a world premiere, *7th Street Echo*, a go-go music play set in Congress Heights developed in partnership with the Go-Go Museum in Anacostia.

Host Joni's program "To Heal DC" devotes the hour to Vernon Eugene Hawkins (May 6, 1939 – July 2, 2025), a Washington DC organizer who ran voter registration drives in 12 states, served as a key behind-the-scenes force alongside Mayor Marion Barry, and directed the Commission on Social Services' HIV/AIDS response in the 1980s — training 1,000 staff members and coordinating with health commissioner Reed Tuckson. His daughter Laverne Hawkins Jones, along with colleagues Saleem Hilton and Norm Nixon, recount how Hawkins built Unifest, a street festival on Martin Luther King Avenue in Anacostia that ran from roughly the early 1980s into the 2000s with five stages of entertainment and health and social services outreach, and how he mentored generations of DC activists — his circle called themselves the Vernonites — while deliberately choosing never to run for elected office, telling his family, "That's not my role." Nixon also announces that a scholarship fund in Hawkins's name at Union Temple Baptist Church distributed $16,000 to students the previous day, including grants directed specifically to HBCU attendees.

Guyanese parliamentarian and maritime attorney Amanza Walton told host Julianne Malveaux that the MV Barima ferry disaster — which left roughly 77 dead and 50 still unaccounted for inside the sunken vessel — was entirely preventable: replacement ships procured from India and Greece have sat idle for years because the government failed across two procurement cycles to finish the stellings needed to dock them, and one of those vessels is now reportedly used by Guyana's First Lady to host galas. Walton also revealed that the government disbanded its ferry inspectorate unit in 2021 and that the National Assembly's speaker has banned parliamentarians from using the word "corruption" on the floor. The second segment features Katie Sanson of the National Women's Law Center explaining that the EEOC — acting on a priority lifted directly from the labor chapter of Project 2025 — has proposed eliminating the EEO-1 data collection requirement that has tracked workforce composition by race, sex, and job category since the 1960s, with a public comment period open through August 24th at regulations.gov.
